progeny

PRODJ-uh-nee -- Latin pro- ('forth') plus gignere ('to bring into being'): what a parent brings forth. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Progeny is the descendants or offspring of a parent.

The old apple tree and all its progeny still grow along the fence line.

Worked Example

A single pair of rabbits released on an island in 1890 leaves behind, a century later, thousands of animals grazing every hillside -- every one of them descended from those two.

All the offspring that come from a parent, and their offspring in turn, are its progeny. Unlike 'family,' which includes parents and cousins, progeny points only downward, to what comes after.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

heirs: Heirs are the people who inherit -- money, titles, or duties -- from someone who came before them. Progeny is purely biological: the offspring of a parent, and their offspring in turn. A childless king's heir might be his nephew, but his progeny could only be his own descendants.

brood: A brood is one batch of young raised together -- a hen and her chicks, a fox and her kits. Progeny has no such limit: it covers all the young a parent produces, and their young after them. One nest holds a brood; five generations of farm cats can be one queen's progeny.

posterity: Posterity means future generations considered as a whole -- the people who will come after us and look back. Progeny belongs to a particular parent: its own offspring and theirs in turn. We preserve photographs for posterity; a grandmother counts her progeny around the table.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ancestors: the people or animals a line came from

forebears: earlier generations of a family

Where it sits · how many generations it reaches — offspring → progeny → descendants

offspring vs. progeny: Offspring is narrower than progeny -- offspring usually means the immediate young of a parent, while progeny can stretch across many generations.

descendants vs. progeny: Descendants is the widest word of the three: progeny most often names what one parent produced, while descendants can reach centuries down a family line to people no ancestor ever met.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forth, forward (Latin)

root — -gen-

root — -gen-: to be born, to bring into being (Latin (gignere, genus))

suffix — -y

suffix — -y: noun-forming ending (state, thing) (Latin (via French -ie))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin pro- ('forth') plus gignere ('to bring into being') plus the noun ending -y -- progeny is literally what has been 'brought forth,' from the same gen- root behind generation and genetics.

Use the root in a new word: genealogy

Use the root in a new word: genealogy: A cousin traced the family's genealogy back six generations to a village in Portugal.

Root Check

Word Choice

Progeny is a formal, slightly literary word and it takes a plural verb ('the progeny were sold at auction'). It fits animals, plants, and people equally well, and it is sometimes stretched playfully to ideas or inventions: 'the progeny of the first computer.'
